extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters learning courtroom/newspaper reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Examples and model copy showing how newspapers report criminal and civil court matters — including trial testimony, verdicts, judicial opinions, civil-accident narratives, insanity commitments, and receivership proceedings. Useful as a guide for writing or teaching court reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include direct courtroom Q&A and testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Report verbatim or closely paraphrased witness testimony and the question-and-answer exchanges that occur on direct and cross-examination, including observable details about demeanor and timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shows a Q&A about Becker telling the witness not to light a match, whether the apartment was dark, and ends noting that the direct examination ended at 11:02 A.M., occupying only twenty-seven minutes. Use short quoted answers and note procedural markers (who asked, who answered, time taken).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report verdicts and statutory punishment ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: State the jury's verdict and, where applicable, the legal range of punishment the convicted person faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Koch story notes the jury took nine minutes and that the crime is punishable by imprisonment in the state penitentiary from one to ten years. Include verdict speed when noteworthy and the statutory or expected sentence range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide defendant's prior history and aliases
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize the defendant's relevant past history, previous convictions, aliases, prior suits or claims, and patterns of behavior that illuminate the current charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Koch article recounts a multi-year pattern of false-injury claims under names like C. F. Post, C. F. Pantle, C. F. Jones, Clarence F. Main, prior convictions, settlements, and arrests in several states — use such background to explain motive/pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize court opinions and articulate the legal test
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting appellate or judicial decisions, summarize the court's legal reasoning and, if given, quote the rule or test the court applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Appellate Division opinion is quoted: 'The test of liability in such cases depends upon the question whether the injury was committed by the authority of the master...' and cites Gervin vs. N.Y. Central R. R. Co. Report the controlling legal test and its application to the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe factual background and injuries in civil suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a clear factual account of accidents or injuries: where and when they happened, immediate results, medical findings, and the practical consequences for the injured party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Florence Lemoine piece describes stepping off a sidewalk, slipping, later being pronounced to have spinal trouble and paralysis, where she was staying, and how the injury affected her stage career. Include location, date, medical opinions, and economic/personal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note procedural posture and motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify procedural steps in the case (appeals, motions for judgment notwithstanding the verdict, reversals) so readers understand the litigation status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the city asked for judgment notwithstanding the verdict; Judge Kesler denied it; the city appealed and the supreme court affirmed. Report such motions, rulings, and their effect on the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify parties, attorneys, and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Name the litigants and their lawyers, and where relevant their offices or affiliations, to clarify who is involved and who is arguing the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories identify Attorney John W. Hart, Abraham Oberstein (299 Broadway), and law firms such as Denny & Denny. Include counsel names and client roles when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include human-interest details and personal color
rubrics_metrics.description: Use humanizing details (demeanor, family background, habits, quotations about feelings) to make legal stories relatable and vivid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Koch's 'blank, fixed expression', his family background, and the account that 'whiskey brought about his ruin' add color. The Baptiste Bardoli narrative (wine bottles, letters to the consul, reunion with his father) is another model. Use such details judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report administrative and regulatory opinions with practical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When officials or administrative officers issue opinions, summarize the legal conclusion and explain practical implications for affected parties or industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Attorney General's opinion that excess fare cannot be collected unless provision is made for refund is presented with his reasoning and its effect on railroad practice. Include the legal rationale and likely operational consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide chronology and timeline of events
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay out the sequence of actions and dates across the history of a case or a subject's pattern of conduct so readers can follow causation and development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Koch narrative lists incidents from 1906 to 1914 with dates, places, amounts collected, arrests and incarcerations. Use clear chronological ordering and dates to show pattern and progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report financial figures and corporate causes in receivership/insolvency cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Include specific sums, creditor exposures, stock issues, and asserted causes for financial distress when covering corporate legal proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Robert Z. Link & Co. receivership story cites nearly $2,500,000 of bank paper, a $1,000,000 preferred stock issue, $600,000 cash on hand, and an estimated $1,000,000 needed — and discusses alleged inflated sales and lack of checking systems. Provide figures and link them to alleged causes.
